Objectives:
Much of the project area vegetation is composed largely of the sagebrush/grass type, with significant areas of the mountain shrub type (serviceberry, antelope bitterbrush, mountain mahogany, etc.) and aspen. These vegetation types in the area are rated in fuels condition classes I, II and III. Fuels in classes II and III are no longer within ecological limits and are susceptible
to large wild fires. The use of prescribed fire can convert class II and III fuel types to class I types, which are within ecological limits and are not susceptible to large or damaging wildfires. The current composition of fuels condition classes is estimated to be Class I 15%, Class II 65% and Class III at 20%.

The project area lies within the area of highest wildfire occurrence in the entire Southwestern Zone. Watershed conditions and rangeland health although satisfactory are less than ecological potential. Plant community diversity has been reduced with the succession of sagebrush and juniper communities. Unique vegetation types such as mountain shrub and aspen are in danger of being replaced by sagebrush due to interspecific competition.

Prescribed fire can and has been used to improve water quality (long-term) by reducing overland flow of water, increasing ground cover and increasing infiltration levels, all of which reduce the amount of sediment that will reach streams. Sediment transported to streams by accelerated rates of erosion is a primary source of elevated levels of dissolved salts. Excess sedimentation and salinity are both issues in the Flaming Gorge Reservoir downstream of the project area. Flaming Gorge provides locally, regionally and nationally significant recreational activity particularly in the use of the fisheries it provides. As water infiltration is improved, spring flows will increase. Any water supplied to Sage Creek from spring flows would be cooler, and more constant in flow rates producing larger base flows in the late summer when the critical period for aquatic wildlife generally occurs. Springs can also be an important source of water for terrestrial wildlife.

Most mountain shrubs (mountain mahogany, serviceberry, etc.) sprout after a fire. Prescribed fire can be used to remove competition from sagebrush and juniper allowing for re-sprouting of the mountain shrubs and increasing production and age class diversity.
Planned_Implementation:
The BLM proposes to treat with prescribed fire, approximately 9,000 acres within the Salt Wells Basin (Map 1). The entire burn block (Maximum Management Area, MMA) encompasses approximately 35 ,000 acres and includes approximately 700 acres of private land (Janets' Inc.) and 3,560 acres of State of Wyoming Trust land. Janet Scarpelli, president of Janets&$ Inc. has
agreed to allow deeded lands under their ownership, within the project area, to be included in the burn. Mrs. Scarpelli is the only State of Wyoming grazing lessee, and has signed a consent form, for approval by the Wyoming State Land Board. The Salt Wells Basin Prescribed Burn is planned for the fall (October) of 2006.

Vegetative communities targeted for treatment include sagebrush/grass, mountain shrub, and aspen, small areas of juniper encroachment (where young junipers are expanding into sagebrush/grass types) may also be included.

To accomplish vegetation and habitat management objectives, the actual burned area will not exceed approximately 10,500 acres of the 35 ,000-acre block (30%).

Objectives: Reduce fuel loading and modify future fire behavior. Reduce fire suppression costs and aid in fire control should a future wildfire event occur within the proposed project area. Reduce the threat to public and firefighter safety. Minimize the loss of important ecosystem components from wildfire events.
Planned_Implementation: The project area would be scheduled to be broadcast burned in the spring months or late fall when existing snow load drifting on leeward slopes can be utilized for fire spread control lines. Implementation would occur over a 3-10 year period, starting as early as the fall of 2019. Ignitions would be accomplished by use of a vehicle-mounted terra-torch where possible (along roads), by hand carried drip torches (areas of limited access such as steep draws, bowls, ridges, and where control may be difficult), and by helicopter with a Heli-torch or plastic sphere dispenser (PSD, areas difficult to access and deemed unsafe for hand ignitions). The majority of the treatment units within the project area would be hand ignited with drip torches.\r\nConstructed control lines would be created with hand tools, black lines (burning), water/foam (wet lines), or the use of a skid steer with mowing attachment. A cultural clearance has been completed for the project area, and any soil disturbing control lines constructed not been previously identified would require site-specific clearances.
